standard.title: Chance Experiments and Simulations
standard.description: design and conduct repeated chance experiments and simulations, using digital tools to compare probabilities of simple events to related compound events, and describe results
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can calculate relative frequencies from data to estimate probabilities of compound events involving 'and', inclusive 'or' and exclusive 'or' (AC9M9P02). They have not yet designed and conducted their own simulations using digital tools to compare simple and compound event probabilities.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students design and conduct repeated chance experiments and simulations using digital tools, comparing simple and compound event probabilities and describing results.

nodes.label: Designing a chance experiment or simulation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can design a chance experiment or simulation that will generate data to compare the probability of a simple event to a related compound event.
nodes.minimum_width: Design one simulation (manual or digital) to investigate a compound probability question; state what data will be recorded and how the simulation replicates the real event.
nodes.typical_width: Design experiments and simulations for a range of compound probability questions; specify the number of trials; identify what data to collect; ensure the simulation correctly models the probability structure (correct outcome space, with/without replacement as appropriate).
wider: Design a simulation to investigate a counterintuitive probability result (e.g. probability that at least two people in a group share a birthday for small group sizes) and explain the design rationale
Investigate how real-world simulations are used in risk modelling and forecasting — discuss what makes a simulation a reliable model
Compare manual (physical) and digital simulation approaches — discuss the advantages of digital tools for large numbers of trials
success_criteria: Specifies the outcome space, what is recorded, and the number of trials
Correctly models the probability structure (with/without replacement, equal/unequal probabilities)
Explains how the simulation replicates the real event

nodes.label: Conducting the experiment and comparing probabilities
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can conduct a repeated chance experiment or simulation using digital tools, compare results for simple and compound events, and describe results.
nodes.minimum_width: Conduct a simulation with at least 50 trials using a digital tool; calculate the relative frequency of a simple event and one related compound event; compare the two results.
nodes.typical_width: Conduct repeated simulations with sufficient trials to see convergence; compare probabilities of simple and compound events (with and without replacement); describe results including what the simulation reveals about the relationship between simple and compound probabilities; compare experimental and theoretical probabilities.
wider: Use repeated trials of First Nations Australian children's instructive games (e.g. Gorri) to calculate probabilities of winning and not winning — compare experimental results from simulation to theoretical predictions derived from systematic listing
Conduct two versions of the same experiment (with and without replacement) using digital tools and compare the effect on compound event probabilities
Investigate how increasing the number of trials affects the closeness of experimental to theoretical probability — connect to the law of large numbers conceptually

response_modes.reason: Students commonly interpret small-sample simulation results as definitive (confusing experimental variability with theoretical probability). Running simulations under different conditions — varying trial counts, with/without replacement — builds understanding of when and why experimental results diverge from theoretical expectations.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The convergence of experimental to theoretical probability as trial count increases is one of the most powerful ideas in probability — visible, verifiable, and conceptually deep. Students who observe and explain this convergence develop genuine probabilistic intuition that goes far beyond mechanical calculation.
success_criteria: Conducts the simulation with a sufficient number of trials (at least 50) using a digital tool
Correctly calculates relative frequencies for both the simple and compound events
Compares the two results and describes what the comparison reveals

nodes.label: Describing and evaluating results
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe simulation results, compare experimental to theoretical probabilities, and explain any discrepancies.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare one experimental (simulation) probability to the corresponding theoretical probability; explain one reason why the results might differ.
nodes.typical_width: Compare experimental probabilities from simulation to theoretical probabilities; describe the relationship between simple and compound event probabilities revealed by the simulation; explain why experimental and theoretical results differ, and what would reduce the discrepancy.
wider: Evaluate the reliability of simulation results across different trial counts — present results from 10, 50, 200 and 1000 trials and discuss convergence
Discuss and evaluate the use of simulation in real-world contexts (e.g. insurance risk modelling, weather forecasting) — assess what makes a simulation trustworthy
Connect simulation results to the design of fair games and discuss what probability results reveal about whether a game is fair

response_modes.reason: Describing and evaluating results integrates the full investigation cycle: design, conduct, compare and explain. The integration challenge is connecting what the simulation shows to what it means probabilistically — moving from 'I got 0.48' to 'this is consistent with a theoretical probability of 0.5 because...' This is the descriptor's full demand.

success_criteria: States the experimental probability and the corresponding theoretical probability
Explains why the two values are unlikely to be identical for a finite number of trials
Identifies what aspect of the design or trial count could be changed to reduce the discrepancy
